rv.q: Theatre Company has just such a precious stone in Tony Kushner's 'Angels in America,' an astonishing seven-hour epic whose power hasn't dimmed since its two parts were first staged in the early 1990s.
Dressed up in the latest digital wizardry, it becomes a memorable, even unforgettable experience.
Unfortunately, the show itself, directed by Sarah Frankcom, was blander stuff: less mind-bending spectacle, more earnest meditation.
Whether or not An Ark is a truly original experiment, its results are dispiritingly bland.
Neither Simons’ lyricism nor producer Todd Eckert’s pioneering mixed reality will work for everybody.
Nonetheless, the overall experience proves haunting.
But despite all the hoopla about the innovative technology, the play’s still very much the thing here, and this is a sweet one.
You are open-minded enough to applaud the effort of Eckert and director Sarah Frankcom, but you are not convinced that this is an endeavor worth pursuing.
For all the supposedly novel tech involved, it’s a rather dull experience.
Ark feels like an example of tech for its own sake.
As beguiling as these actors are – and they are an exquisite ensemble – they are not provided with much of a hook to pull us in and hold us close.
While it’s fascinating to complicate a near-future in which theater can survive without actors physically present, An Ark remains more a proof-of-concept curiosity than a revelation.

cn.t: Mixed-reality experiment featuring holographic Ian McKellen divides critics: some praise the intimate, innovative tech, while others find the gimmick overshadows Simon Stephens' thin narrative.
